classification.difficultyReason: Reconstruct two branch rules from a graph, select their domains and recognise that the left branch admits a possible rule rather than a uniquely determined gradient from labelled points.

inlines.text: Find a possible rule for the following.

spec.sourceRegion: Left column, question 34, graph beneath the instruction.
spec.description: Unshaded Cartesian graph with positive-axis arrowheads. Two blue rays meet at a filled point (-1,1). The left ray extends upwards-left; the right ray descends through (0,1/2) and (1,0), continuing downwards-right. Dashed black guides join the junction to both axes. There is no third branch or endpoint marker at x=1.

leftBranch.qualification: Only the junction is numerically identified on this ray. Its reconstructed slope is a possible choice consistent with the source appearance, not an additional printed numerical given.

spec.answerVisibility: The complete supplied graph remains visible in the question. Branch equations and explanatory annotations are not printed on it.

answer.short:
One possible rule is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-x&x<-1,\\-\frac12x+\frac12&x\ge-1.\end{cases}$$

Use the labelled intercepts for the right branch; $y=-x$ is one possible left-branch rule.
answer.worked:
The right branch passes through $(0,\frac12)$ and $(1,0)$, so
$$\begin{align*}m&=\frac{0-\frac12}{1-0}\\m&=-\frac12\\y&=-\frac12x+\frac12.\end{align*}$$
Only one point is labelled on the left ray. A possible rule consistent with its appearance is $y=-x$, which passes through $(-1,1)$.

Both rules give $y=1$ at $x=-1$, so the included junction can belong to the second branch. One possible rule is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-x&x<-1,\\-\frac12x+\frac12&x\ge-1.\end{cases}$$
